Patient Vignette: A.P.

A.P. is a 22-year-old, single, South Eastern Asian male and a full-time university student. He presents as quiet and watchful, his posture rigid, as if bracing for a blow. He speaks in a low, measured tone, often pausing to scan the room before continuing.

He tells me about his deployment nine months ago. As a volunteer with a humanitarian aid organization, he spent four months in a conflict zone. He was a logistics coordinator, tasked with ensuring the safe passage of food and medical supplies to besieged communities. He describes the constant, low hum of drones overhead, the sudden, percussive sound of shelling, and the smell of dust and cordite that seemed to cling to everything. The event that broke him, he says, was not a single explosion, but a morning in a field hospital. A child, no older than six, was brought in after a strike. He had shrapnel wounds. A.P. was asked to hold the boy’s hand while the medics worked. The boy’s eyes were wide, unblinking. He didn’t scream. He just stared at A.P. and said, “It hurts.” A.P. held his hand until the boy stopped breathing.

Now, back in his university city, A.P. cannot escape that moment. He is a student of international relations, a field he once loved. Now, he cannot sit through a lecture. The moment a professor mentions military strategy or civilian casualties, his heart hammers against his ribs. He feels a cold sweat break out on his palms. He has to leave. He spends most of his time in his cramped apartment, the blinds drawn. The sunlight is too bright, a harsh, accusing glare. The sound of a motorcycle backfiring sends him diving behind his sofa, his breath ragged. He describes it as a complete loss of control, a terrifying regression.

He has stopped answering calls from his family. His mother, worried, left him a voicemail asking about his classes. He listened to it three times, but could not bring himself to call back. The words felt stuck in his throat. He feels a profound sense of isolation, a gulf between himself and everyone else. His friends talk about exams, parties, and future careers. He listens, but it feels like a foreign language. He thinks, They don’t know. They can’t know. He has a recurring nightmare. In it, he is back in the field hospital, but the boy is older, with A.P.’s own face. The boy reaches out and says, “You didn’t help me.”

He avoids all news reports. He has deleted all social media apps from his phone. He cannot bear to see images of conflict. He has started drinking alone at night, a cheap whiskey he buys from the corner store, just enough to blur the edges. He says it’s the only way he can fall asleep before the nightmares come. He describes a constant feeling of being on edge, a hypervigilance that exhausts him. He cannot focus on his studies. He has failed two midterms. He sits in the back of the library, his back to the wall, watching the door.

He came to see me because his academic advisor, concerned about his failing grades and his vacant, haunted look, strongly suggested it. A.P. says he doesn’t know if talking will help. He feels like he is living in a glass bubble, watching the world from a distance. He is a student who cannot study, a son who cannot call his mother, a young man who cannot escape the ghost of a child he held as he died. He is trapped in the aftermath of a moment that has not ended.
